CONSTRUCTIVE EVICTION AND THE COVENANT OF QUIET ENJOYMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Riverbend Properties, LLC

WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes two connected bodies of California law: the covenant of quiet enjoyment that is implied in every lease, and the doctrine of constructive eviction that California courts built on top of that covenant. It is being prepared in connection with the tenancy of Jordan Lee at 742 Alder St., Apt. 3, Sacramento, CA 95814 in Sacramento County, under a rental agreement or lease with Riverbend Properties, LLC. The conduct or condition at issue is recorded as: Heating shut off building-wide from December 3 onward, and a locked stairwell blocking the only entrance to the unit. Each clause below reports what a named Civil Code section or a named published California opinion says — what the implied covenant is, what kind of interference breaches it, who can commit the interference, what a tenant’s surrender of possession does to the obligation to pay rent, what measures of damages the authorities discuss, and where the doctrine sits next to other landlord-tenant statutes. This sheet does not evaluate the tenancy at 742 Alder St., Apt. 3, Sacramento, CA 95814, does not decide whether anything described above occurred or how serious it was, and does not tell anyone what to do.

THE COVENANT IMPLIED IN EVERY LEASE (CIV. CODE § 1927)
Civil Code section 1927, enacted in 1872 and never amended, is one sentence: "An agreement to let upon hire binds the letter to secure to the hirer the quiet possession of the thing hired during the term of the hiring, against all persons lawfully claiming the same." It sits in the Civil Code’s chapter on hiring in general, so it speaks of a "letter" and a "hirer" rather than a landlord and a tenant. The Court of Appeal in Andrews v. Mobile Aire Estates (2005) 125 Cal.App.4th 578 described the relationship between that section and the broader covenant the courts apply: the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment is "partially codified" in section 1927, the statutory covenant guarantees the tenant against the rightful assertion of a paramount title, and "Beyond the statutory covenant, the landlord is bound to refrain from action which interrupts the tenant’s beneficial enjoyment." Andrews also states the rule that the covenant is implied in the absence of contrary language, and Erlach v. Sierra Asset Servicing, LLC (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th 1281 states that the covenant "is breached upon actual or constructive eviction of the tenant." Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 261 describes how the covenant grew: it once protected the lessee against physical interference only, and in more recent years it has been read to insulate the tenant against acts or omissions of the landlord, or of anyone claiming under the landlord, that interfere with the tenant’s use and enjoyment of the premises for the purposes contemplated by the tenancy. Nothing in these authorities is specific to the lease between Jordan Lee and Riverbend Properties, LLC.

THE THRESHOLD: SUBSTANTIAL INTERFERENCE, NOT MINOR ANNOYANCE
The published decisions draw a line between interference that breaches the covenant and interference that does not. Andrews v. Mobile Aire Estates states: "Minor inconveniences and annoyances are not actionable breaches of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment. To be actionable, the landlord’s act or omission must substantially interfere with a tenant’s right to use and enjoy the premises for the purposes contemplated by the tenancy." The phrase "for the purposes contemplated by the tenancy" ties the standard to what the particular premises were let for; the examples Andrews collects include a landlord who installed interior building supports that interfered with a tenant’s billiards business and a landlord who denied a retail tenant the adjoining parking spaces essential to its use of the property. Andrews also states, in a footnote, that because the covenant is present in every lease absent contrary language, cases involving commercial tenants apply equally to residential tenancies. Whether the conduct or condition recorded for 742 Alder St., Apt. 3, Sacramento, CA 95814 — Heating shut off building-wide from December 3 onward, and a locked stairwell blocking the only entrance to the unit — crosses that threshold is a question of fact this sheet does not answer.

THE LANDLORD’S SUBJECTIVE INTENT IS NOT AN ELEMENT
Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 261 states that "It is not necessary to show that the landlord acted with the subjective intent to compel the tenant to leave the property or deprive the tenant of quiet enjoyment." The same passage describes a presumption that a landlord intends the natural and probable consequences of the landlord’s acts, so that where those acts effectively deprive the tenant of the use and enjoyment of the premises, an intent to evict is implied from the character of the acts done. That rule matters for how a claimed constructive eviction is proved: under these authorities the inquiry is directed at the effect of the landlord’s acts or omissions rather than at the landlord’s state of mind. This sheet reports the rule and does not characterize anything Riverbend Properties, LLC did or did not do.

WHO CAN COMMIT THE INTERFERENCE — AND WHOSE CONDUCT FALLS OUTSIDE THE COVENANT
Andrews v. Mobile Aire Estates states: "The perpetrator of the interference with the tenant’s quiet enjoyment need not be the landlord personally. There may be an actionable breach where the interference is caused by a neighbor or tenant claiming under the landlord." The same opinion marks the outer edge of that principle in a footnote: the covenant runs between the tenant and the landlord from whom the tenant rents, so nuisance activities on neighboring premises "not owned or controlled by the aggrieved tenant’s landlord" may interfere with a tenant’s quiet enjoyment without amounting to a breach of the covenant as between tenant and landlord. Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. collects the same distinction from older authority, quoting the rule that a lessor "is responsible upon the covenant for his own acts, and for the acts of others claiming by title paramount to the lease, but he is not responsible for the acts of a mere trespasser." The same passage also quotes the California Supreme Court for the proposition that "a landowner cannot interfere with his tenant’s possession or enjoyment by allowing others to enter upon the land." Who owns or controls the property from which the conduct recorded above originates is a factual question about 742 Alder St., Apt. 3, Sacramento, CA 95814 that this sheet does not resolve.

WHAT MAKES AN INTERFERENCE A CONSTRUCTIVE EVICTION: SURRENDER OF POSSESSION
Constructive eviction is the label the cases give to a breach of the covenant that the tenant answers by giving up the premises. The California Supreme Court stated the rule in Kulawitz v. Pacific Woodenware & Paper Co. (1944) 25 Cal.2d 664: "Any interference by the landlord by which the tenant is deprived of the beneficial enjoyment of the premises amounts to a constructive eviction if the tenant so elects and surrenders possession, and the tenant will not be liable for rentals for the portion of the term following his eviction." Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. quotes the same doctrine in the form that a disturbance depriving the tenant of beneficial enjoyment amounts to a constructive eviction "provided the tenant vacates the premises within a reasonable time." Erlach v. Sierra Asset Servicing, LLC states the rule with the same timing element. The Supreme Court had earlier said in Standard Livestock Co. v. Pentz (1928) 204 Cal. 618 that "the covenant of quiet possession in a lease is not breached until there has been an actual or constructive eviction." Nativi quotes that statement while noting that some authorities recognize that a tenant may sue for breach of the covenant while remaining in possession. Green v. Superior Court (1974) 10 Cal.3d 616 describes the practical consequence of the surrender requirement in the residential context: the doctrine "gives little help to the typical low income tenant today because to avail himself of the doctrine a tenant must vacate the premises." Whether Jordan Lee has surrendered possession of 742 Alder St., Apt. 3, Sacramento, CA 95814, and when, are facts this sheet does not establish.

Andrews v. Mobile Aire Estates sets out the consequences the decisions attach to each path. Pacific Woodenware & Paper Co. states the rent consequence of the first path in the same terms: the tenant "will not be liable for rentals for the portion of the term following his eviction." THE MEASURE OF DAMAGES: CIVIL CODE SECTIONS 3300 AND 3304, AND A DISAGREEMENT ABOUT SECTION 3304
Two Civil Code sections are named in the decisions on this subject. Section 3300 provides that "For the breach of an obligation arising from contract, the measure of damages, except where otherwise expressly provided by this Code, is the amount which will compensate the party aggrieved for all the detriment proximately caused thereby, or which, in the ordinary course of things, would be likely to result therefrom." Section 3304 prescribes a specific measure — the price paid to the grantor or a proportion of it, interest for the period the grantee derived no benefit, and expenses properly incurred in defending possession — for breach of a covenant of "seizin," "right to convey," "warranty," or "quiet enjoyment" in a grant of an estate in real property. The authorities do not line up on whether section 3304 reaches leases. In Standard Livestock Co. v. Pentz (1928) 204 Cal. 618 the California Supreme Court concluded that section 3304 "was never intended to have reference to leases of real estate or to the detriment caused by breaches of covenants for the peaceable possession of leased premises." Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 261 states that section 3300 supplies the measure of contract damages for breach of the covenant implied in a lease, citing Standard Livestock. Andrews v. Mobile Aire Estates (2005) 125 Cal.App.4th 578, by contrast, states in the text that section 3304 prescribes the measure of damages for breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment and adds that case law allows a tenant to recover contract damages under section 3300, listing lost profits, lost business goodwill, and moving expenses as possible recoveries in an appropriate case. This sheet reports what each source says and calculates nothing for Jordan Lee.

THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO TERMINATE (CIV. CODE § 1932) AND THE DOCTRINE’S INDEPENDENCE FROM THE REPAIR STATUTES
Alongside the judicially developed doctrine, the Civil Code contains its own termination provision. Section 1932 provides that the hirer of a thing may terminate the hiring before the end of the agreed term in two situations. The first is "When the letter does not, within a reasonable time after request, fulfill his obligations, if any, as to placing and securing the hirer in the quiet possession of the thing hired, or putting it into good condition, or repairing". The second is when the greater part of the thing hired, or the part that was the material inducement to the contract, perishes other than through the hirer’s want of ordinary care. The section is worded in terms of a request followed by a reasonable time. The California Supreme Court in Green v. Superior Court (1974) 10 Cal.3d 616 described the relationship between the common law doctrine and the Civil Code’s repair provisions: California courts "have evolved the “constructive eviction” doctrine as a common law remedy completely independent of this statutory framework"; under the modern decisions, the same opinion says, a tenant’s right to terminate has been measured not by the standards of sections 1941 or 1942 but by a developing standard keyed to whether the landlord’s acts or omissions rendered the premises unfit for the purposes for which they were leased. Whether any request was made to Riverbend Properties, LLC, and what followed, are facts outside this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: Two Civil Code sections are named in the decisions on this subject. Section 3300 provides that "For the breach of an obligation arising from contract, the measure of damages, except where otherwise expressly provided by this Code, is the amount which will compensate the party aggrieved for all the detriment proximately caused thereby, or which, in the ordinary course of things, would be likely to result therefrom." Section 3304 prescribes a specific measure — the price paid to the grantor or a proportion of it, interest for the period the grantee derived no benefit, and expenses properly incurred in defending possession — for breach of a covenant of "seizin," "right to convey," "warranty," or "quiet enjoyment" in a grant of an estate in real property. The authorities do not line up on whether section 3304 reaches leases. In Standard Livestock Co. v. Pentz (1928) 204 Cal. 618 the California Supreme Court concluded that section 3304 "was never intended to have reference to leases of real estate or to the detriment caused by breaches of covenants for the peaceable possession of leased premises." Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 261 states that section 3300 supplies the measure of contract damages for breach of the covenant implied in a lease, citing Standard Livestock. Andrews v. Mobile Aire Estates (2005) 125 Cal.App.4th 578, by contrast, states in the text that section 3304 prescribes the measure of damages for breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment and adds that case law allows a tenant to recover contract damages under section 3300, listing lost profits, lost business goodwill, and moving expenses as possible recoveries in an appropriate case. This sheet reports what each source says and calculates nothing for Jordan Lee.

expectedJSON.body: Alongside the judicially developed doctrine, the Civil Code contains its own termination provision. Section 1932 provides that the hirer of a thing may terminate the hiring before the end of the agreed term in two situations. The first is "When the letter does not, within a reasonable time after request, fulfill his obligations, if any, as to placing and securing the hirer in the quiet possession of the thing hired, or putting it into good condition, or repairing". The second is when the greater part of the thing hired, or the part that was the material inducement to the contract, perishes other than through the hirer’s want of ordinary care. The section is worded in terms of a request followed by a reasonable time. The California Supreme Court in Green v. Superior Court (1974) 10 Cal.3d 616 described the relationship between the common law doctrine and the Civil Code’s repair provisions: California courts "have evolved the “constructive eviction” doctrine as a common law remedy completely independent of this statutory framework"; under the modern decisions, the same opinion says, a tenant’s right to terminate has been measured not by the standards of sections 1941 or 1942 but by a developing standard keyed to whether the landlord’s acts or omissions rendered the premises unfit for the purposes for which they were leased. Whether any request was made to Riverbend Properties, LLC, and what followed, are facts outside this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: The decisions treat a landlord’s use of legal process differently from physical interference. Nativi v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. states: "Where a landlord does not physically interfere with tenants’ possession and merely wrongfully serves a notice to quit, tenants can recover damages for a wrongful eviction only if the landlord acted with malice." The same passage states that a mere threat to resort to legal process, made in good faith, "cannot amount to a constructive eviction." Nativi takes that phrase from the California Supreme Court’s decision in Lindenberg v. MacDonald (1950) 34 Cal.2d 678. Nativi nonetheless held that a triable issue of fact existed as to whether the letter threatening an unlawful detainer action in that case was issued in good faith or was part of a larger course of conduct amounting to constructive eviction. Whether any notice or letter directed to Jordan Lee was served, and with what state of mind, are questions of fact this sheet does not reach.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code section 1940.2 makes certain landlord conduct unlawful when done "for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling." One listed item ties directly to the covenant discussed in this sheet: it is unlawful to "Use, or threaten to use, force, willful threats, or menacing conduct constituting a course of conduct that interferes with the tenant’s quiet enjoyment of the premises in violation of Section 1927 that would create an apprehension of harm in a reasonable person. Nothing in this paragraph requires a tenant to be actually or constructively evicted in order to obtain relief." A tenant who prevails in a civil action, including one in small claims court, to enforce rights under the section is entitled to a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. The section also provides that a good-faith oral or written warning notice about conduct that violates or may violate the rental agreement, rules, or laws is not a violation of the section, and that the section neither enlarges nor diminishes a landlord’s right to terminate a tenancy under existing state or local law. The section therefore describes a statutory penalty that operates without the surrender of possession the constructive eviction doctrine requires; it does not describe anything about the tenancy of Jordan Lee.
